newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Lebed says Russia's rulers must go.
newsitem.headline: Lebed says Russia's rulers must go.

text.p: Russian presidential hopeful and former security chief Alexander Lebed said on Friday the Kremlin's current rulers had to go because their policies risked bloodshed and social upheaval.

Lebed, one of Russia's most popular politicians who polled strongly in last year's presidential elections, said Russia was paralysed in a state of "pseudo-democracy" and that 1997 would be a crucial year.

"This low-level party nomenklatura which came to power on the first wave of reforms must go. Otherwise, there will be social upheaval and a lot of bloodshed," he told a news conference during a private visit to Geneva.
"The system that exists in Russia today is dying. This year will be a watershed for the history of Russia."
Lebed, former secretary to Russia's powerful Security Council who was sacked by ailing President Boris Yeltsin last October, arrived in Switzerland on a two-day visit on Friday.
He will have informal talks with the Swiss Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Jakob Kellenberger, on Saturday and return home the same day.
Lebed has no official post but he has been trying to boost his credibility in the West with recent trips to the United States, Germany and France.
At home, the former general and paratrooper appeals to millions of Russians as an honest soldier who stopped the war in breakaway Chechnya, where he brokered a peace deal last year.
Lebed, who once said he admired Chile's dictator Pinochet in a Russian newspaper interview, criticised Russian reforms and promised to boost confidence in the economy if he came to power.
"Eighty percent of my people live beyond poverty line. It's total paralysis," he said.

"We need to reform this system, our customs, taxation. We've got a huge army of bureaucrats prospering on illegal activities. Everyone is busy in Russia trying to deceive the state. We have no rules of the game. It's like the law of the jungle," he said.
"The essence of my policy would be to eliminate all these obstacles. But we have to act in a civilised way to prevent the country from sliding into social explosion," he said without elaborating.
Lebed's answers to questions about his political future and programme were equally vague.

Asked what would happen on the Russian political arena if Yeltsin died, which means an election must be held within three months according to Russia's constitution, Lebed said: "We believe that the next president will find it easier to govern."
"So many errors and mistakes were made...that any step will be a step towards progress."
